question: What is the main job of your nasal cavity when you breathe in air?

options.A: To store excess air during heavy exercise
options.B: To produce sound waves for vocalization
options.C: To exchange oxygen directly into the bloodstream
options.D: To warm, humidify, and filter incoming air

explanation: Spot on! Your nose acts like a natural air conditioner, warming, cleaning, and moistening the air before it travels down into your lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why is the epiglottis such an important little flap in your throat?

options.A: It separates the nasal cavity from the oral cavity
options.B: It regulates the speed of airflow into the lungs during exercise
options.C: It prevents food and liquid from entering the trachea during swallowing
options.D: It produces mucus to trap dust particles in the nasal passages

explanation: You got it! The epiglottis acts like a clever trapdoor, closing over your windpipe when you swallow so food goes safely down your food pipe instead. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h1)

question: What stops your windpipe (trachea) from squishing or collapsing when you breathe?
explanation: Exactly! Those sturdy C-shaped cartilage rings keep your airway open wide and clear at all times. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h2)

question: If someone accidentally swallows or breathes in a small object, why is it more likely to go down the right bronchus?

options.A: The left bronchus is blocked by the heart's position
options.B: The right bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical
options.C: The right lung has three lobes instead of two
options.D: Air flows at a much faster speed on the right side

explanation: Correct! The right main tube makes a much straighter, wider path down from the windpipe, making it an easier slipway for anything unwanted. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h2)

question: What is the key job of the special fluid called surfactant in your lungs?

options.A: To reduce surface tension and prevent alveolar collapse
options.B: To bind oxygen molecules directly for transport
options.C: To moisten the trachea and primary bronchi
options.D: To trap dust and bacteria entering the deep lungs

explanation: Brilliant! Surfactant keeps the tiny air sacs from sticking together and collapsing on themselves when you breathe out. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h3)

question: Why is the membrane inside the lungs where gas exchange happens so incredibly thin?

options.A: To allow the lungs to stretch easily during inhalation
options.B: To reduce the overall weight of the thoracic organs
options.C: To prevent white blood cells from entering the alveoli
options.D: To allow fast and efficient diffusion of gases

explanation: Spot on! A super thin wall means oxygen and carbon dioxide can zip back and forth between your lungs and blood instantly. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h3)

question: What actually makes air rush into your lungs when you take an inhalation?

options.A: Intrapulmonary pressure drops below atmospheric pressure
options.B: Surfactant expands the alveolar volume rapidly
options.C: Atmospheric pressure drops below intrapulmonary pressure
options.D: The diaphragm relaxes and pushes the chest upward

explanation: You nailed it! When your chest gets bigger, the pressure inside drops lower than the outside air, sucking air naturally right in. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h4)

question: Which muscle does most of the heavy lifting when you take a normal, quiet breath in?
explanation: Correct! The dome-shaped diaphragm is your main breathing muscle, moving down to pull air into your chest effortlessly. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h4)

question: How is the vast majority of oxygen carried around your body in the blood?

options.B: Dissolved directly in the blood plasma
options.C: Attached to white blood cell membranes
options.D: Bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells

explanation: You got it! Hemoglobin inside your red cells acts like a fleet of tiny delivery trucks carrying oxygen everywhere it's needed. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h5)

question: If a patient has severe anemia with very low hemoglobin, what is the most direct problem this causes?

options.A: Complete cessation of carbon dioxide production
options.B: Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood
options.C: Inability of the diaphragm to contract properly
options.D: Immediate collapse of alveolar air sacs

explanation: Spot on! Fewer delivery trucks (hemoglobin) mean the blood just can't pack and carry enough oxygen to the body tissues. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h5)

question: Where in the brain is the main control center that keeps your breathing rhythm on autopilot?
explanation: Correct! The brainstem quietly manages your breathing rhythm in the background so you don't have to think about it. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is the main chemical trigger in your blood that tells your brain it is time to breathe?

options.C: Carbon dioxide levels in the blood
options.D: Oxygen levels in the arterial blood

explanation: You got it! A buildup of carbon dioxide is the strongest alarm bell your body uses to say 'time to take a breath.' [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h6)

question: During a quick nursing assessment, which of these is an early warning sign that a patient is struggling to breathe?

options.A: Use of accessory muscles to breathe
options.B: Warm and dry skin on the extremities
options.C: A slow and irregular heart rate

explanation: Spot on! When breathing gets tough, patients start using their neck and shoulder muscles to help pull air in. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h7)

question: If you hear fine crackling sounds in a patient's lower lung fields using your stethoscope, what does that usually mean?

options.D: Severe spasm of the vocal cords

explanation: Brilliant! Those crackles happen when tiny, fluid-filled or sticky air sacs pop open as the patient breathes in. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h7)
